chapter: Postwar years, accident and lean times
title: Learning to walk again, and refusing special treatment
summary: Learning to walk with the uneven leg was hard; he refused chairs and favors on jobs to prove he could earn his place, and says critics now praise his playing.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Did you have trouble after you got to the point where you started walking again, was it difficult
learning to walk? With the difference in your leg?
Yes, very, very. With the difference in your leg, and used to moving, you know, being a guy who's act --
You were a fast man.

Oh, yeah. Fact, fast as I am -- I used to try to bos a little bit, and you find out you're not able to do those thing because you can't move like you -- once, like you want to, and fast enough, and what happens, you -- you make yourself almost ill because you get mad at yourself because you can't do what you want to do.

And should be doing. You know what you should be doing, but you can't do it. So now it's a matter of accepting that you've got a -- once you accept it, and people call up, all right, Dad, all right, Pops, all right, Grandy, you know, what they mean, and then you figure -- you say well gee, I'm being honored. They're very nice.
You know, once you accept that, then that begins to you look at the guy who's saying that, and he's old -- your old -- he's older than you. Yeah, you know, I mean well, you say okay. Well.
Did you get adjusted finally? I mean to a point that it didn't bother you, although I would assume that it -- just physically it was a problem moving around, wasn't it?
Well that --
Up and down on stands, and things like that?

That, and you you had to get adjusted to, because a lot of jobs I could get on, even now. They'd say well, would you need a high chair? Would you need a chair? Can we get you anything? Can we get you a -- I say no. For a heck of a long time I wouldn't do it, because I wanted to prove, and let the agents, or the boss, or what the -- who in the hell he was, to know, I was capable of earning my own, and I didn't want any different -- don't -- you know what I'm trying to say.
Yes.
Don't make any difference --
No favors.

No favors. No. Don't make any difference. Say well, Mr. Autrey, we would pay you this, but after all, you such and such and such and such, I said want you to know I'm selling my horn. Never mind my broken leg, or what-not. I'm okay, you know. And play, and I have been -- thank God I have been able to do it. In fact, in the last few years a lot of the authorities, guys say well Herman, my playing has been much better, and has been in so many years, and they say that the critics, say I'm still right now, age and whatnot, better than this one or that one, or so and so and so and so.
Because in -- in my lipping of the horn.
And I've been able to play this, and play that, and do a lot of things that so far other guys have not been able to do, which I'm glad that I'm still being accepted, and able to play. You know.

Did you find that because once you were walking, but you walked with a limp, insofar, just as getting jobs were concerned, was there any kind of prejudice against you, do you feel, because of that? Even though, obviously, that has nothing to do with your playing.
Well -- I'm trying to think. Vaguely I want to say -- I want to say yes, because it's all -- my disability there, I mean not being able to do this, or they had a little doubt, maybe.
A doubt. Yes, this is what I'm wondering.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. And they come up, well can we get you this? Don't you need that? Don't you need the other? And I say well no. The hell with it. No, I'm okay.
You want to be accepted as --
Yes. I didn't want -- I don't want people to say oh get him -- put a bed down for Pops, you know. And drink this, and because he's -- after all, he has a bad
leg. I say man, never mind the damn leg. Just blow. And I've been able to blow out -- blow out many, God damn it, I play --
(Laughter.)
